lessons.title: When a Company Cannot Repay: Defaults, the IBC and Lessons from Real Cases

children.text: Almost nobody wakes up one morning in default. A company slides towards it over several quarters, through a sequence of stages that are visible to its bank long before they are admitted internally. Understanding that sequence is the difference between a company that renegotiates from a position of some strength and one that loses control of itself entirely.

body.text: Default is a process, not an event. Control passes from the promoters gradually, through overdue days and covenant breaches, and then all at once when a tribunal admits the case.

children.text: The Slide: How Indian Lenders Classify Stress
The RBI requires banks to classify accounts by how overdue they are, well before they become a formal problem. A borrower should track the same clock.

body.title: From one missed date to non-performing

events.title: SMA-0
events.description: Principal or interest overdue by up to 30 days. The account is flagged internally and reported. Nothing public happens yet.

events.title: SMA-1
events.description: The relationship manager escalates. Expect questions, site visits and a request for a repayment plan.

events.title: SMA-2
events.description: Serious. The bank is now preparing for the possibility of classification, and credit bureaus and other lenders can see the stress.

events.title: Non-performing asset
events.description: The bank must provide capital against the loan. Fresh lending effectively stops, and recovery teams take over from relationship teams.

children.text: A
special mention account
is not yet a default in the legal sense, but it changes who inside the bank is handling your file. Once an account becomes a
non-performing asset
, the economics for the bank change, and so does its willingness to be flexible.

markDefs.definition: An RBI classification for accounts overdue but not yet non-performing: SMA-0 up to 30 days, SMA-1 from 31 to 60 days and SMA-2 from 61 to 90 days.
A loan on which interest or principal has been overdue for more than 90 days. The bank must then set aside capital against it, which changes its behaviour towards the borrower.

body.title: The line that changes everything
body.textWithBlank: A loan account is classified as a non-performing asset once interest or principal has been overdue for more than ___ days.
body.explanation: The 90-day mark forces the bank to set aside capital against the loan. That provisioning cost is why a bank that was willing to discuss restructuring at day 60 becomes far more rigid at day 100.

children.text: What a Company Can Still Do Before It Is Too Late
Between stress and insolvency there is a window, and almost every useful option lives inside it.
Refinance.
Replace an expensive or short loan with a cheaper or longer one, while your financials still support a fresh sanction.
Restructure.

Under the RBI's Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets, lenders can agree a resolution plan: extended tenure, a moratorium, reduced instalments, or conversion of part of the debt to equity.
Promoter infusion.
Fresh equity from promoters is often the price lenders demand for any concession, and it signals commitment.
Sell assets.
A non-core plant, a piece of land or a division, sold deliberately, beats the same asset sold at distress prices later.
One-time settlement.
Negotiate a discounted lump sum to close the account, usually only available when the lender has largely given up on full recovery.

body.title: Two ways companies handle the same stress

columns.label: The approach that usually works
points: Tells the lender early, with numbers and a plan
Shares a realistic downside case, not only a recovery case
Brings promoter money or a concrete asset sale to the table
Deals with all lenders in parallel, not one at a time
Accepts tighter monitoring in exchange for time

columns.label: The approach that usually fails
points: Waits for the lender to notice
Presents optimistic projections that are missed again next quarter
Asks for time with nothing offered in return
Pays the loudest lender and ignores the others, triggering cross-defaults
Treats the problem as temporary until it is structural

body.text: Diverting money between group companies, delaying supplier payments to service a loan quietly, or drawing down limits just before a known breach are the three moves that turn a solvable problem into a fraud investigation. A restructuring can be negotiated. A finding of diversion of funds cannot be.

children.text: The IBC: What Happens When the Window Closes

The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 changed Indian corporate borrowing more than any other reform of the last decade, because for the first time a default could cost promoters the company itself. A financial or operational creditor can apply to the National Company Law Tribunal once a default crosses the prescribed threshold, currently ₹1 crore.
Admission.
The NCLT admits the application. From this moment the promoters are no longer in charge.
Moratorium.
Under Section 14, all recovery actions, suits and enforcement against the company are frozen, which also gives the business breathing space to keep operating.
Interim resolution professional.
An insolvency professional takes over management of the company. The board stands suspended.
Committee of creditors.
Financial creditors form the CoC and effectively control the outcome from here.
Resolution plans.
Bidders submit plans. A plan needs at least 66% of the CoC voting share to be approved, then NCLT approval.
Outcome.
Either an approved resolution plan and a new owner, or liquidation, with proceeds distributed in the order set out in Section 53.
The
moratorium
and the
committee of creditors

are the two features founders underestimate. The moratorium protects the company from being torn apart by individual creditors, but it also means the promoters cannot sell assets to fix the problem themselves. And once the CoC exists, the promoters are usually just spectators to decisions about their own company.

markDefs.definition: The freeze under Section 14 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code once a case is admitted. No recovery suit, enforcement or asset transfer can proceed against the company.
The body of financial creditors formed after admission, which votes on resolution plans. A plan needs at least 66% of voting share to be approved.

children.text: The Code sets 180 days for the process, extendable by 90, with an outer limit of 330 days including litigation. Reality is different.

stats.label: Average time to resolution
stats.context: As on 31 March 2026, against a 330-day outer limit

stats.label: Overrun against the Code
stats.context: More than a year beyond the statutory limit

body.label: What creditors actually recover
body.value: Recovery rates have hovered around a third of admitted claims, and fell sharply in FY26
body.context: CARE Ratings put recoveries at about 32% in the third quarter of FY26, while ICRA reported that recoveries against admitted claims dropped to roughly 23% in 2025-26 from 46% the previous year. Recovery under liquidation is far worse, at low single digits. The averages move a great deal from quarter to quarter depending on which large cases resolve, so treat any single figure as a snapshot.

children.text: Four Cases That Teach Different Lessons

cells: ArcelorMittal's plan provided ₹42,000 crore upfront plus ₹8,000 crore of equity infusion, upheld by the Supreme Court in 2019
Secured financial creditors recovered about 92% of admitted dues. Unsecured financial creditors received roughly 4%
Tata Steel paid ₹35,200 crore against debt of over ₹56,000 crore
About 63% recovered, a haircut of roughly 37%
Twin Star Technologies offered ₹2,962 crore against admitted claims of about ₹64,838 crore. The NCLAT later set the approval aside
Under 5% recovery, reported at the time as a haircut of about 96%
A resolution plan was approved in 2021 but never implemented. In November 2024 the Supreme Court used Article 142 to order liquidation
The ₹200 crore infused by the successful applicant was forfeited and a ₹150 crore bank guarantee invoked

body.title: Recovery against claims in three resolved cases (%)
Calculate the haircut
body.prompt: Twin Star offered ₹2,962 crore against admitted claims of about ₹64,838 crore in the Videocon case. What percentage of their claims would creditors have recovered? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ₹2,962 crore divided by ₹64,838 crore is about 4.6%, meaning a haircut of over 95%. The NCLAT set the approval aside, but the episode remains the reference point in India for how little can be left by the time a case is resolved.

body.text: Compare Essar and Videocon. Same Code, same tribunal system, wildly different outcomes. The difference was the underlying asset: a modern steel plant that two global buyers wanted, against a group of consumer electronics businesses with little operating value left by the time the process ended. The Code recovers what the business is worth, not what the lenders are owed. Time destroys that value, which is why the 744-day average matters so much.

body.label: The promoter is not necessarily protected
body.value: SBI moved to invoke personal guarantees of about ₹15,000 crore from the Ruias in the Essar case
body.context: Personal guarantees given by promoters survive the corporate insolvency process, and Part III of the Code allows lenders to proceed against personal guarantors separately. Losing the company does not automatically end the promoter's liability, which is the single strongest argument for treating a personal guarantee as a major decision rather than a signature at the end of a sanction letter.

body.title: What the moratorium does
body.question: A company is admitted to insolvency. One of its suppliers has already obtained a court decree for unpaid dues and wants to enforce it. A bank wants to auction the mortgaged factory under SARFAESI. What happens?
options: Both can proceed, since their claims predate admission
Both are frozen by the moratorium under Section 14 while the process runs
Only the bank can proceed, because it is secured
Only the supplier can proceed, because it has a decree
body.explanation: The moratorium stops suits, enforcement and asset transfers against the company so the business can keep operating as a going concern and be sold whole if possible. Secured status and an existing decree do not override it. Creditors are instead paid through the resolution plan or, failing that, the liquidation waterfall.

body.title: Who actually decides?
body.question: Two resolution plans are on the table for a company in insolvency. The promoters strongly prefer one. Who decides which plan is adopted?
options: The promoters, as the original owners
The committee of creditors, by at least 66% of voting share, with the plan then approved by the NCLT
body.explanation: Control shifts to the financial creditors on admission. The CoC votes, needing at least 66% voting share, and the NCLT then approves the plan. Promoter preference carries no weight in the vote, and promoters of defaulting companies are often barred from bidding for their own company under Section 29A.

body.title: The liquidation waterfall, in plain order

children.text: If no resolution plan succeeds, the company is liquidated and the proceeds are distributed in the priority order set out in Section 53 of the Code. Simplified:
Insolvency resolution process costs and liquidation costs.
Workmen's dues for 24 months and secured creditors who gave up their security to the pool, ranking equally.
Employee wages and dues for 12 months.
Financial debts owed to unsecured creditors.
Government dues and any remaining amounts owed to secured creditors who enforced their security.
Any remaining debts and dues.
Preference shareholders.
Equity shareholders.

Read the last two lines again. Shareholders are behind every creditor, every employee and the government. In most Indian liquidations they receive nothing at all, which is the concrete version of the point made back in Chapter 1: equity is the residual claim.

body.title: The first bad quarter
body.scenario: You are the CFO of a ₹200 crore revenue auto ancillary company in Aurangabad. A major customer has cut orders by 40%, and your projections show that in five months you will not be able to pay both the ₹1.8 crore monthly term loan instalment and your suppliers. Payments are current today. The company has three lenders: a public sector bank with the term loan and a charge on the factory, a private bank with working capital limits, and an NBFC with an equipment loan. Both directors have given personal guarantees to the public sector bank.
body.prompt: Write the plan for the next five months.
body.modelAnswer:
Month 1, establish the facts:
1. Build a weekly 26-week cash flow, not a monthly annual budget. In stress, the weekly view is the only one that tells the truth.
2. Read all three agreements for covenants, cross-default clauses and the exact definition of an event of default. A breach with one lender may trigger the others.
3. Quantify how much of the shortfall is temporary (one customer) against structural (pricing, capacity, fixed cost base).

Month 1 to 2, act on what you control:
4. Attack working capital before debt. Collections, inventory, and supplier terms typically release more cash faster than any refinancing.
5. Identify a non-core asset that can be sold deliberately now rather than desperately later.
6. Take the numbers to the board and ask the promoters directly whether they will infuse funds and how much. Lenders will ask this within the first ten minutes of any conversation, and the personal guarantees mean the directors are exposed regardless.
7. Pursue replacement revenue. A restructuring based only on cost cuts is a weaker case than one with a named new customer.

Month 2 to 3, approach the lenders together:
8. Go to all three with the same pack and the same request, before any payment is missed. Approaching one at a time invites each to protect itself at the others' expense.
9. Ask for something specific: a six-month moratorium on principal with interest serviced, or a stretched tenure that reduces the instalment to a level the weekly cash flow supports.
10. Offer something concrete in return: promoter infusion, the asset sale proceeds, a tighter reporting cadence, or additional security if it genuinely exists.

Throughout:
11. Never let an account cross 30 days overdue while a restructuring discussion is live. Classification changes the bank's incentives against you.
12. Do not divert funds between group companies or pay one lender out of another's security. This is the point where a business problem becomes a personal legal problem.
13. Keep the auditor and the board informed in writing. Surprises at year end damage credibility exactly when you need it.

The objective for these five months is not to solve everything. It is to stay in the window where you are still negotiating, rather than being processed.

body.title: Early warning signs that a company is sliding
steps: Working capital limits are fully drawn month after month, with no swing back
Supplier payments are being stretched to make loan payments
Covenant headroom has fallen for two consecutive quarters
Interest is being paid out of fresh borrowing rather than operating cash
One customer accounts for a large share of revenue and is slowing down
The finance team is producing numbers late, or the auditor is asking new questions
Promoters are being asked to give more personal security for the same facilities

body.label: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India
body.description: The regulator's site carries the Code, regulations and quarterly newsletters with the actual data on cases admitted, resolved, timelines and recovery rates. Worth reading one newsletter to see how wide the range of outcomes really is.

cards.definition: RBI stress classifications for accounts overdue up to 30, 60 and 90 days.
A loan overdue beyond 90 days, against which the bank must provide capital.
Agreed changes to loan terms under the RBI's Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets.
The 2002 Act letting a secured creditor take possession of and sell secured assets without a court suit.
The corporate insolvency resolution process under the IBC, triggered by a default above the prescribed threshold.
The Section 14 freeze on suits, enforcement and asset transfers once a case is admitted.
Financial creditors who vote on resolution plans, needing at least 66% voting share.
The liquidation priority order, with equity shareholders last.

points: Default arrives in stages: SMA-0, SMA-1, SMA-2 and then NPA classification beyond 90 days overdue.
Almost every useful option, from refinancing to restructuring to a planned asset sale, exists only before classification hardens.
Under the IBC, admission removes the promoters from control and hands the outcome to the committee of creditors.
The Code sets an outer limit of 330 days, but average resolution took about 744 days as on 31 March 2026.
Recoveries have averaged around a third of admitted claims and vary hugely by case: about 92% for Essar Steel's secured creditors, under 5% in the Videocon plan.
Personal guarantees survive corporate insolvency, and lenders can pursue promoters separately.
Equity shareholders sit last in the liquidation waterfall and usually receive nothing.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or tax advice. Insolvency law and RBI classification norms are summarised, not stated exhaustively, and both change. Case figures are drawn from public reports at the time of each event, and several of these cases involved subsequent appeals and revisions. Take professional advice on any actual situation of financial stress.
